## The Problem

This is a **regression problem**: we want to predict a numeric target $y$ from two inputs, $x_1$ and $x_2$, using the data below.

| $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $y$ |
|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| 1 | 0 | -2 |
| 2 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | -2 | -1 |
| 4 | 3 | 1 |

Consider these four models:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Model A:} \quad \hat{y} &= -2 + 0.5 x_1 + 0.25 x_2 \\
\text{Model B:} \quad \hat{y} &= -1.25 + 0.25 x_1 + 0.25 x_2 \\
\text{Model C:} \quad \hat{y} &= -0.5 + 0 x_1 + 0.25 x_2 \\
\text{Model D:} \quad \hat{y} &= -0.5 + 0 x_1 + 0 x_2
\end{aligned}
$$

Each model has the form $\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2$. Its total squared loss is

$$L(w_0, w_1, w_2) = \sum (\hat{y} - y)^2$$

LASSO adds a penalty on the size of the slopes $w_1$ and $w_2$. The best model is the one with the smallest **objective**:

$$\text{Objective} = L(w_0, w_1, w_2) + \alpha \left( |w_1| + |w_2| \right)$$

The number $\alpha$ sets how strong the penalty is. The intercept $w_0$ is not penalized.

## Questions

You need only arithmetic for this problem. Show your work, and give exact decimals rather than rounding.

**Question 1.** Which of the four models is best when $\alpha = 0$? With $\alpha = 0$ there is no penalty, so this is the ordinary linear model.

**Question 2.** Which of the four models is best when $\alpha = 4$?

**Question 3.** Which of the four models is best when $\alpha = 7$?

**Question 4.** Which of the four models is best when $\alpha = 10$?

**Question 5.** As $\alpha$ increases, what happens to the slopes of the best model?

## Solution

**Start by calculating the loss of each model.** For Model A:

| Row | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $y$ | $\hat{y} = -2 + 0.5 x_1 + 0.25 x_2$ | $\hat{y} - y$ | $(\hat{y} - y)^2$ |
|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | -2 | $-2 + 0.5 + 0 = -1.5$ | 0.5 | 0.25 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | $-2 + 1 + 0.25 = -0.75$ | -0.75 | 0.5625 |
| 3 | 3 | -2 | -1 | $-2 + 1.5 - 0.5 = -1$ | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 4 | 3 | 1 | $-2 + 2 + 0.75 = 0.75$ | -0.25 | 0.0625 |

Adding the last column gives $L = 0.875$. The other models work the same way:

| Model | $\hat{y}$, row 1 | $\hat{y}$, row 2 | $\hat{y}$, row 3 | $\hat{y}$, row 4 | $L$ | $\lvert w_1 \rvert + \lvert w_2 \rvert$ |
|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| A | -1.5 | -0.75 | -1 | 0.75 | $0.25 + 0.5625 + 0 + 0.0625 = 0.875$ | $0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75$ |
| B | -1 | -0.5 | -1 | 0.5 | $1 + 0.25 + 0 + 0.25 = 1.5$ | $0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5$ |
| C | -0.5 | -0.25 | -1 | 0.25 | $2.25 + 0.0625 + 0 + 0.5625 = 2.875$ | $0 + 0.25 = 0.25$ |
| D | -0.5 | -0.5 | -0.5 | -0.5 | $2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5$ | $0 + 0 = 0$ |

**Then calculate each objective,** $L + \alpha \times (\lvert w_1 \rvert + \lvert w_2 \rvert)$. The smallest in each column is in bold.

| Model | $\alpha = 0$ | $\alpha = 4$ | $\alpha = 7$ | $\alpha = 10$ |
|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| A | **0.875** | $0.875 + 4(0.75) = 3.875$ | $0.875 + 7(0.75) = 6.125$ | $0.875 + 10(0.75) = 8.375$ |
| B | 1.5 | $1.5 + 4(0.5) =$ **3.5** | $1.5 + 7(0.5) = 5$ | $1.5 + 10(0.5) = 6.5$ |
| C | 2.875 | $2.875 + 4(0.25) = 3.875$ | $2.875 + 7(0.25) =$ **4.625** | $2.875 + 10(0.25) = 5.375$ |
| D | 5 | $5 + 4(0) = 5$ | $5 + 7(0) = 5$ | $5 + 10(0) =$ **5** |

**Question 1.** Model A is best at $\alpha = 0$, with objective 0.875. It has the smallest loss, and it uses both inputs.

**Question 2.** Model B is best at $\alpha = 4$, with objective 3.5. It uses both inputs, with a smaller slope on $x_1$ than Model A.

**Question 3.** Model C is best at $\alpha = 7$, with objective 4.625. It uses only $x_2$.

**Question 4.** Model D is best at $\alpha = 10$, with objective 5. It uses neither input and predicts $-0.5$, the mean of $y$, for every row.

**Question 5.** The slopes shrink toward 0, and they reach exactly 0.
